prize_parts.citation: For the development of general palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling
For the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of DNA bases without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: Pd-catalysed C-N coupling is the clearest case on the shortlist of a method that changed how chemists everywhere build bonds: aryl amines went from a hard, substrate-limited transformation to a routine one, through systematic ligand design by Buchwald and Hartwig. Its adoption is documented in a vast number of syntheses, in medicinal chemistry and in industrial process routes, after three decades of independent confirmation. Pairing it with base editing gives the prize both a molecule-making half and a chemistry-of-life half. In base editing the new chemical idea is concrete: a tethered deaminase performs a defined nucleobase transformation at a programmed site, and the adenine editor needed directed evolution of a deaminase to act on DNA. That makes it a chemical invention rather than only a use of a genome-editing tool. Liu as sole laureate for the second part matches the attribution most of us accept, and keeps the union at three people.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to B054 is that the 2010 prize for Pd cross-coupling already honoured the area, and C-N coupling can be read as a ligand-driven extension of the Heck, Negishi and Suzuki chemistry. Kosugi's earlier tin-amide coupling is a genuine priority issue. For B018, the 2020 CRISPR prize and the early clinical stage argue for waiting, and Nishida and Kondo (Target-AID) have an independent priority claim that a Liu-only citation does not cover. Combining two unrelated achievements may also look like splitting the prize to reach a majority rather than a coherent statement.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks B054 third and B018 first, arguing that Buchwald and Hartwig are a clean two-laureate pair, that Kosugi is only a precursor, and that base editing is a single-laureate chemical idea distinct from CRISPR.
responses.response: I agree on both halves, and his Liu-only attribution for base editing is the reason I would not add Komor and Gaudelli to my configuration. On the 2010 overlap he is more relaxed than I am. The 2010 prize rewarded C-C bond formation, and C-N coupling needed its own ligand classes and mechanistic understanding, so it is a different bond-forming problem. I accept that this novelty argument is not yet settled in the committee. Kosugi's tin-amide work was narrow, toxic-tin-based and not general, which is why I keep him off the list.

responses.point: Zou ranks B024 (perovskites) first and B054 second, valuing the structure-property story of perovskite solar absorbers and calling C-N coupling a method a whole community adopted.
responses.response: I share her view of B054 and her note that the C-N chemistry is distinct from 2010. I disagree on ranking perovskites above it. Efficiency records are impressive, but stability and lead toxicity are unresolved, six credited names have disputed priority, and much of the progress is device engineering rather than one chemical discovery. Cross-coupling has long been proven where perovskites have not.

responses.point: Chabes ranks B018 first and treats base editing as deamination chemistry turned programmable, with Liu, Komor and Gaudelli as the coherent trio, while flagging Kondo and Nishida's priority and prime editing overlap.
responses.response: I accept his chemical framing, which is what convinced me to put B018 in my own configuration. I would still credit Liu alone: Komor and Gaudelli did the decisive bench work, but the prize should name the person who conceived and drove the programme, and a three-name slot is better spent on B054. A trio for B018 would not fit beside two names for B054 under the three-person limit, so I would then favour B018 as a stand-alone prize rather than a two-part one. His caution about Kondo and Nishida is fair and unresolved.

responses.point: Aili ranks PROTACs (B023) first, calling induced proximity a clear molecular design principle, while noting that Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli's PROTAC lineage is separate from the cereblon glue branch and no degrader is yet approved.
responses.response: I see the design principle and hold B023 as my first alternative. My reservations are as he states them: the PROTAC and cereblon-glue strands are two discoveries with different people, and the clinical proof is incomplete. A prize that has to explain why only the PROTAC trio is credited invites the attribution dispute he describes. I would want the committee to decide whether the chemical novelty is the heterobifunctional design or the glue mechanism before I rank it above established methods.

responses.point: Linke ranks massively parallel sequencing (B058) first, calling it a scalable chemical-physical measurement that transformed genomics, while asking what is new relative to Sanger sequencing and how to split Solexa and 454 credit.
responses.response: I agree the impact is beyond doubt, and the reversible-terminator chemistry is real molecule-level chemistry, so B058 is my second alternative. His own question about Sanger, together with the split between Solexa and 454 lineages and Mayer's role, is the reason I cannot rank it first. I think the committee would have to pick the chemistry (Balasubramanian and Klenerman) and say plainly that the platform lineages are left out.

uncertainties: Whether the 2010 Pd cross-coupling prize leaves enough room for C-N coupling in the view of a majority of members.
Whether Kosugi deserves a slot or merely a mention for the precursor tin-amide coupling.
Whether base editing is judged mature enough and sufficiently separate from the 2020 CRISPR prize, and how to handle the Nishida and Kondo priority claim.
Whether a two-part prize combining synthetic methodology with chemical biology will be accepted as coherent.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My mentor Masamune, my institutions (Chalmers, KTH, Lund, Tartu) and my Lund colleagues Linke and Sparr are not tied to any shortlisted credited name that I know of. I lean toward the synthetic-methodology candidate because of my own field, which colleagues should weigh.
